title: Client-Owned Orchestration of One Business Operation
pattern: Client applications (mobile, web, CLI) coordinate a single business operation by issuing multiple mutations against separate backend services themselves, rather than calling one server-side operation. This couples every client to the internal service layout and, when several clients exist, duplicates the same workflow knowledge in each of them.
why_bad: Clients become tightly coupled to the internal backend structure: any change to the workflow or to a backend service requires coordinated updates and releases across all client codebases, which makes service rewrites and migrations risky. A client that loses connectivity or fails mid-sequence leaves the operation partially executed, exposing inconsistent state.
detection: Client-facing code that performs several sequential write mutations across separate downstream service endpoints to complete one use case. Subcases: (a) a single client importing and coordinating multiple disjoint services instead of consuming a unified use-case endpoint; (b) multiple client applications (web, iOS, Android) each reproducing the same fine-grained call sequence for the same use case.
counterexample: A simple system with a single client and stable backend services, where the indirection buys little. Highly custom admin panels or developer tools that intentionally require low-level, independent control of separate subsystems.
fix: Introduce a server-side Coordinator/Manager operation (a coarse-grained API facade) that owns the orchestration sequence and returns the use-case result through one endpoint. Give that operation the failure and consistency semantics the workflow needs (explicit compensation or recovery across independent services); rely on a local transaction only when its resource boundary actually allows one, since a facade does not by itself make cross-service mutations atomic.
source: Righting Software, Chapter 2, "Decomposition - Clients Bloat and Coupling" [54, 55, 541]; *Righting Software* by Juval Löwy (2019), p. 21, 493.
